description_full: IRSA Inversiones y Representaciones Sociedad Anónima, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the diversified real estate activities in Argentina. The company operates through five segments: Shopping Malls, Offices, Sales and Developments, Hotels, and Others. It is involved in the acquisition, development, and operation of shopping malls, office buildings, and other non-shopping mall properties primarily for rental purposes; and lease and service related to rental of commercial space and other spaces. The company also acquires and operates luxury hotels and resorts under the Intercontinental, Libertador, and Llao Llao names; develops, constructs, and sells residential properties, including apartment tower complexes; and acquires undeveloped land reserves for future development or sale. In addition, it engages in the development and operation of stadium; provision of ¡appa!, a digital loyalty platform; development, maintenance, and sale of undeveloped parcels of land and/or trading properties; and provision of room, catering, and restaurant services. The company was incorporated in 1943 and is headquartered in Buenos Aires, Argentina. IRSA Inversiones y Representaciones Sociedad Anónima operates as a subsidiary of Cresud S.A.C.I.F. y A.

financial_summary: IRSA Inversiones Y Representaci is a small-cap real estate business with a $1.1B market cap on $361M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are contracting by -6.9pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at -2% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 55% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $195M in free cash flow — roughly 54 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.33× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 3.8×.

Management returns a meaningful 12.9% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 37% operating margin runs 14pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.85x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-32.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 34% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 42% and a beta of 0.84, it moves roughly with the market.
About $2.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 60% in the 2020 crash, 38% in the 2022 bear market and 80% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 65% below its DCF fair value of $36.27, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 39%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $28.72 to $46.68 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Real Estate peers: P/E 7.3 vs 23.6, EV/EBITDA 3.3 vs 16.3 and P/FCF 5.5 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 18.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $21.87 on average, 74% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 11.0% annual cash-flow growth, 17pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 2% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 3.24).
It runs a 55% gross margin and converts 54% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.33x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 54%.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.1x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 25pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.4x net debt to EBITDA ($313.0M of cash against $512.1M of debt), with interest covered 3.8x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.86 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 14.2% over 3 years and -22.6% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 58%).
Free cash flow has compounded -11.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of -13.7% a year over five years.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.1%, and institutions hold 20%.
It returns 12.9% a year to shareholders (12.9% in dividends).
The share count has grown 7.9% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
